meta.title: Japanese — First Words
meta.subtitle: 69 greetings, particles and everyday basics — after hiragana, before N5
meta.desc: The words a beginner needs before any word list: greetings and courtesies (こんにちは, ありがとう, すみません), the copula and the polite endings (です, だ, ます), the particles every sentence is held together by (は, が, を, に, で, の…), and a handful of words for people, time and money (さん, 円, 時, 日本). 69 notes, each with TWO cards (Japanese → English, English → Japanese), each scheduled on its own, in a teaching order rather than by frequency. Study after hiragana and before JLPT N5; five to ten new cards a day finishes it in three to six weeks. — WHY THESE ARE NOT IN THE N5 DECK: the JLPT lists the level decks are built from follow the pre-2010 test specification, which kept its greetings and particles outside the word list. They place 9 of these words at N3, 6 at N2 and 6 at N1, and 48 (です, が, を, も, 日本語, 母…) at no level at all. Each is carded here once and not again in the level it was listed at. Words N5 and N4 already card (はい, いいえ, どうぞ, the numbers) are left to them. — The card is the vocabulary decks' card: the word as it is written, furigana and Hepburn romaji (the particle は is "wa", へ "e", を "o", and the speaker says them so), the meanings with the dictionary's own note on each sense (for a particle the note is the meaning: "indicates location of action"), and up to three real sentences with furigana and a speaker; 2 have no usable sentence in the corpus. A word whose kanji are not N5 kanji is asked in kana and written in kanji on the back. The reverse card asks with the first sense alone. Nothing here is composed: what the dictionary has no entry for (でした, ました) is not carded. — Readings, meanings, notes on usage and the "usually written in kana" marks: JMdict (Electronic Dictionary Research and Development Group, CC BY-SA 4.0). Furigana: JmdictFurigana (CC BY-SA 4.0). Kanji: KANJIDIC2 (EDRDG, CC BY-SA 4.0) and KanjiVG (Ulrich Apel, CC BY-SA 3.0). The levels named above are those of Jonathan Waller's JLPT lists (tanos.co.uk, CC BY). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR; the readings over them come from segmenting that corpus with MeCab and the UniDic dictionary, so a reading over an example sentence is a machine's and can occasionally be wrong — the headword's own reading is the dictionary's.
